newsitem.title: ICELAND: FEATURE - Iceland glacier flood is unique.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Iceland glacier flood is unique.

text.p: It started as an earthquake, grew into eruptions by an ice-capped volcano and reached a climax when 3,500 billion litres of melt water burst through Europe's largest glacier.

The torrent of sulphurous water pushed hundreds of huge slabs of ice down a black sand plain below Iceland's mighty Vatnajokull glacier. It was an awesome throw-back to Ice Age upheavals some 14,000 years ago.
The torrent smashed a 400-metre (1,300-foot) steel and concrete bridge, damaged another and cut off an economically-vital coastal road in an uninhabitated area of southwest Iceland.

Scientists said this month's natural disaster was a clash of fire and ice that could happen only on Iceland, a windswept North Atlantic island just below the Arctic Circle which bubbles with geothermal activity and is still in the making in a geological sense.

"This is the only area in the world with active volcanoes covered with large ice caps similar to those during the Ice Age," said Helgi Bjoernsson, a professor of glaciology with the University of Iceland in Reykjavik.
"The glacier flood is telling us something about the process during the Ice Age when many mountains around the world were formed by volcanic eruptions breaking through ice caps," he said.
"You see a struggle here between fire and ice. Every now and then volcanoes erupt and melt ice which turns into a flood. Then they become quiet and are covered with ice again. The ice wins."

Bjoernsson said ice would soon cover a crack eight km (five miles) long that opened when the Grimsvotn volcano exploded through the glacier on October 2, three days after an earthquake heralded what was to become Iceland's fastest-running flood this century.
The earthquake started in Bardarbunga, one of three main volcanic centres suppressed by the glacier. But the eruption came from Grimsvotn to the south.
"Somehow they were acting together. The seismic activity took place in a large area," Bjoernsson said.

He has used waves of radio-echo sounding to map out the hidden bedrock topography of the Vatnajokull ice cap, which covers over 8,300 square kilometres (3,200 square miles) and rises more than 2,000 metres (6,560 feet) above sea level.

Water pressure under Vatnajokull had been rising since the volcano first sent ashes and steam high into the air. The eruptions melted part of the ice, filling a sub-glacial lake above Grimsvotn to bursting point within a month.
Bjoernsson said an estimated 3,500 billion litres of water had amassed in the lake, lifting the 250 metre (820 foot) thick ice cap as much as 140 metres (460 feet).
The melt water burst through the glacier on the morning of November 5, and much faster than expected.
"We had to run for our lives when it broke through," said hydrologist Arni Snorrasson, who was measuring river levels at the food of the glacier.
After the flood ended two days later the ice cap, having floated on the melt water for weeks, came crashing down and now rests on the bedrock again.
The lake fills up every five years because ice is continously being melted by geothermal activity, and occasional volcanic activity speeds up the process.
The biggest Vatnajokul flood this century, in 1938, took three days to reach its peak, but this time the torrent did so in 14 hours because the water was warmer, Bjoernsson said.

The volcano went quiet in mid-October but authorities had remained on the alert for an outpouring, closing off the road to traffic each. Tremors on the eve of the flood told scientists something was afoot and they were in an emergency meeting with civil defence authorities when it broke loose.

The bridges were built two decades ago to withstand no more than about 15,000 cubic metres (530,000 cubic feet) per second. At its peak, the flood rushed out at 45,000 cubic metres (1.6 million cubic feet) per second.
Repairing damage will cost an estimated 1.1 billion Icelandic crowns, the equivalent of $16.5 million.
Why build a road and bridges below a towering glacier?
"We have to take chances in this country," Bjornsson said with a wry smile. "We kept monitoring the seismic activity and thanks to science no lives were lost because we gave an early warning."

Iceland's 270,000 citizens, hardy decendants of Viking settlers more than a thousand years ago, are used to natural disasters, from earthquakes to volcano eruptions. The word "Geysir" or geyser, for hot springs, is one of Iceland's linguistic contributions to the world.
Iceland is covered to 11 percent by glaciers with the rest mostly mountains and lava fields resembling a moonscape, except around the coast where most people live.
More eruptions could follow underneath Vatnajokull.
"For 60 years these volcanoes have been suspiciously quiet," said Pall Einarsson, a professor of geophysics.
"But the last year and a half has been a period of unrest. We may see further eruptions somewhere in the glacier in the next few months or years."
